Dear all,

I am running a CFA model using lavaan (version 0.6.16), with ordinal items and the ULS estimator. The model converged regularly after 89 iterations and I did not receive any errors or warnings.

However, I am encountering two issues I’d appreciate help with:

The Chi-square test statistic is reported, but the p-value is NA (as is the p-value for the baseline model).

The standard errors for the residual variances are all zero. Is this expected behavior with ULS and ordinal indicators?

Additionally, I would like to test for residual invariance across groups (or time). Is this feasible under these settings (ordinal data and ULS estimation), and if so, what is the proper way to specify it in lavaan?

Thank you in advance for your help!

Best regards,
Marco

messages.body_plain:
> it does not work
> summary(fit, standardized = c(“std.all”, “std.nox”))
>
> but I find this would work:
> summary(fit, standardized = c(“std.lv <http://std.lv>”, “std.nox”))
>
> it seems that “std.all”, “std.nox” cannot exist in one result.

 Weird, took a minute to track down the problem.  summary() actually does provide std.nox with std.all, but you won't see it printed by the print.lavaan.parameterEstimates() method.

PE <- summary(fit, standardized = c("std.all", "std.nox"))$pe
PE                # std.nox not printed,
PE$std.nox        # but it is there, and
as.data.frame(PE) # it is printed by the print.data.frame() method

@Yves, the issue is lines 415-419 of lav_print.R <https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/blob/master/R/lav_print.R#L418>:

  # if standardized, remove std.nox column (space reasons only)
  # unless, std.all is already removed
  if (!is.null(y$std.all)) {
    y$std.nox <- NULL
  }

Ages ago, lavaan would print all 3 standardized solutions by default, which made the Console output wider than the standard acceptable 80 characters.  Omitting one of the 3 standardized solutions was a way to prevent that.  When you explicitly requested only std.all and std.nox (a feature I added last year), the above logic still removes std.nox unnecessarily.  To prevent that, I could update the print method to only remove it when std.lv <http://std.lv> and std.all are already there:

  # if 3 standardized solutions, remove std.nox column
  if (!is.null(y$std.lv <http://std.lv>) && !is.null(y$std.all)) {
    y$std.nox <- NULL
  }

But I was never in favor of printing std.lv <http://std.lv> by default (which is why I updated the standardized= argument to accept a character string).  In my opinion, when all 3 exist, it would be better to drop std.lv <http://std.lv>:

  # if 3 standardized solutions, remove std.lv <http://std.lv> column
  if (!is.null(y$std.nox) && !is.null(y$std.all)) {
    y$std.lv <http://std.lv> <- NULL
  }

> compRelSEM(fit_secondorder, higher = "Wellbeing", tau.eq = FALSE)

> Wellbeing: 0.787
>
>
> reliabilityL2(fit_secondorder, "Wellbeing")

> omegaL1: 0.7946842
> omegaL2: 0.9017477
> partialOmegaL1: 0.9037898
>
> My Questions:
>
> The reliability values differ depending on the function used.

The reason they differ is because the deprecated reliabilityL2() only calculated model-implied (rather than observed) total variance for the denominator, whereas the more general function gives you the choice.  The highlighted values above would match if you set compRelSEM(fit_secondorder, higher = "Wellbeing", obs.var = FALSE), which tells it to use model-implied total variance in the denominator.

> Also, the subscale reliabilities are different from when I compute them separately with ci.reliability. Which values should I report?

You didn't provide your ci.reliability() output, but that is only in the MBESS package now (it hasn't been part of semTools for several years).  But the point estimates are still provided by the deprecated reliability() function, which confusingly outputs several options that compRelSEM() makes possible but only if explicitly requested.  The reliability() output's "omega2" (also "omega" if the model has simple structure and no residual covariances) is what compRelSEM(obs.var=FALSE) provides, reliability() output's "omega3"  output is what compRelSEM() provides by default.  Also, unlike the deprecated functions, compRelSEM() provides both the higher-order and subscale reliabilities in the same output:

Engagement_LV: 0.683
Perseverance_LV: 0.766
Optimism_LV: 0.714
Connectedness_LV: 0.748
Happiness_LV: 0.893
Wellbeing: 0.787

> Can I compute omega for the global Wellbeing sum score (the average of the subdimensions)?
That is what the highlighted values above represent: reliability of the sum or average of all observed indicators (i.e., the proportion of that composite's variance that is attributable to the higher-order factor).

messages.subject_clean: Comparing Two Models with and without a Latent Interaction Term in Lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I’ve developed two models in lavaan and would like to compare them. The first model includes three predictors, while the second model adds a latent interaction term between two predictors. I used the IndProd function from Semtools to create the interaction variable with a double-mean centered approach.

Model 1 (Without Interaction Term):

Model1 <- '

# Measurement model

Outcome =~ Outcome1 + Outcome2 + Outcome3

Predictor1 =~ Predictor1_1 + Predictor1_2 + Predictor1_3

Predictor2 =~ Predictor2_1 + Predictor2_2 + Predictor2_3

Predictor3 =~ Predictor3_1 + Predictor3_2 + Predictor3_3

# Structural model

Outcome ~ Predictor1 + Predictor2 + Predictor3 '

Model 2 (With Interaction Term):

Model2 <- '

# Measurement model

Outcome =~ Outcome1 + Outcome2 + Outcome3

Predictor1 =~ Predictor1_1 + Predictor1_2 + Predictor1_3

Predictor2 =~ Predictor2_1 + Predictor2_2 + Predictor2_3

Predictor3 =~ Predictor3_1 + Predictor3_2 + Predictor3_3

Interaction_LV =~ Predictor1_1.Predictor2_1 + Predictor1_1.Predictor2_2 + Predictor1_1.Predictor2_3 + Predictor1_2.Predictor2_1 + Predictor1_2.Predictor2_2 + Predictor1_2.Predictor2_3 + Predictor1_3.Predictor2_1 + Predictor1_3.Predictor2_2 + Predictor1_3.Predictor2_3

#Covariances

Predictor1_1.Predictor2_1 ~~ Predictor1_1.Predictor2_2 + Predictor1_1.Predictor2_3 + Predictor1_2.Predictor2_1 + Predictor1_3.Predictor2_1

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

For the first time in 4 years, a new simsem is on its way to CRAN.  There have been a few bug fixes in that time, but CRAN specifically requested some changes to the documentation format that facilitate their move from PDF to HTML manuals on each package's CRAN page.

Unfortunately, this had to happen quite quickly, and did not leave me time to update simsem regarding how it interfaced with runMI() in semTools.  When I sent the new lavaan.mi package to CRAN, I posted about how it would interfere with old semTools workflows <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/n2_5BZkDC8w/m/A339xki9AQAJ>.  It also interferes with simsem workflows that depend on the deprecated feature that allowed users to request multiple imputation (using mice or Amelia) behind the scenes.  You can see an example of an interruption at the link below, as well as a current solution for anyone running a simulation that involves multiple imputation:

https://github.com/simsem/simsem/issues/86

As stated in that thread, the time-senstivity of this release required me to simply remove that functionality from this version (simsem 0.5-17), but I hope to find time this summer to reinstate it as much as possible using the lavaan.mi package.  It is likely that users will have to use the sim(datafun=) argument to impute simulated incomplete data, for which I will make a vignette to illustrate how easy that is (see the example in the link above).  But my goal is to still allow lavaan.mi() or a wrapper like cfa.mi() to be called automatically when users indicate imputations are to be analyzed, so that the automatic extraction of results remains simple from the user's experience.

I appreciate your patience,
Terrence

Dear lavaan-specialists,

I have run into a - to me - somewhat confusing problem.
I am attempting to test a multi level path model similar to a moderated mediation. All variables are observed, my exogeneous variable is categorical (coded -1, 1), my mediators (M1&M2) are continuous, and my outcome is continuous. My moderator (W) is continuous. I have four clusters (overall N = 1400, smallest cluster has 140+ observations) and have specified the same model on Level 1 and 2, as I simply want to account for two individuals from one cluster being more similar to each other than two individuals from different clusters.

My model looks like this:

Level:1
Y ~ b1*M1+b2*M2+cd*X+mod*W+w1*M1:W+w2*M2:W+w3*X:W
M1 ~ a1*X
M2 ~ a2*X

Level:2
Y ~ b1*M1+b2*M2+cd*X+mod*W+w1*M1:W+w2*M2:W+w3*X:W
M1 ~ a1*X
M2 ~ a2*X

If I use the moderator W in its non-centered form (scaled 1-7), the model estimation completes without a hitch.

1: lavaan->lav_lavaan_step11_estoptim(): Model estimation FAILED! Returning starting values.
2: lavaan->lav_lavaan_step11_estoptim(): Model estimation FAILED! Returning starting values.
3: lavaan->lav_lavaan_step15_baseline(): estimation of the baseline model failed.

I would be grateful if someone could help me understand why re-scaling the moderator creates this issue. Also, as I suspect the issue might be with the interactions, would it be an appropriate workaround to just compute the interactions outside lavaan and then use them as regular predictors?

Kind regards,
Lara

messages.body_plain:
> what is the conceptual difference between NLMINB (optimizer) and ML estimator?
> My guess is that the ML define the fitting equation to be maximized...and the NLMINB is part of a numerical method to carry out the estimation?

Correct. ML estimates are obtained by minimizing a loss function (usually the negative log-likelihood), but many optimization algorithms (a couple of which are implemented by the nlminb() function) can be used to find estimates that do so.  But the nlminb() function can also minimize other loss functions (e.g., a sum of squared deviations) to yield other types of estimates (e.g., least-squares), or even to find other types of "best numbers", like optimal weights that maximize reliability of a composite score (see the semTools::maximalRelia() function, which uses the optim() function).

messages.body_plain:
This turned out to be an issue with sam.method = "global" + std.lv <http://std.lv> =
TRUE in general.

Long story short: std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE fixes the latent (residual) variances to
1, and they are never free parameters. But in global SAM, we need to
free up the residual variances of the endogenous/dependent latent
variables in step 2, otherwise, we fix the residual variance to one
while in step 1 (measurement only), we fixed the total variance to one.

I believe this is now fixed in the github version of lavaan (0.6-20.2290)

Yves.

Hi,

I am fitting a three-time-point multigroup latent change score model on a sample of about 3,000. The study has a year gap in observations, so I am specifying a phantom variable to account for the unequal time intervals. I am running into convergence issues, and I feel it concerns how I specify the phantom variables (specifically the constraints) in my model.

Can someone take a look at my model code for a sanity check?

```
for (model_name in names(coupling_models)) {
  cat("model:", model_name, "\n")

  delta <- coupling_models[[model_name]]$delta
  xi <- coupling_models[[model_name]]$xi

  model_code <- paste0('

  ### latent true scores
  pds1 =~ 1*PDSS_fu1
  pds2 =~ 1*PDSS_fu2
  pds3 =~ 1*PDSS_fu4

  dc1  =~ 1*disc_mean_fu1
  dc2  =~ 1*disc_mean_fu2
  dc3  =~ 1*disc_mean_fu4

  ### phantom latent scores
  pds2.5 =~ NA*PDSS_fu2
  pds2.5 ~~ 0*pds2.5
  dc2.5  =~ NA*disc_mean_fu2
  dc2.5 ~~ 0*dc2.5

  ### latent change scores
  dpds2 =~ 1*pds2
  dpds3 =~ 1*pds3
  ddc2  =~ 1*dc2
  ddc3  =~ 1*dc3

  # ### autoregression (fixed) -- removed because i think this is redundant
  # pds2 ~ 1*pds1
  # pds2.5 ~ 1*pds2
  # pds3 ~ 1*pds2.5
  #
  # dc2 ~ 1*dc1
  # dc2.5 ~ 1*dc2
  # dc3 ~ 1*dc2.5

  ### proportional change (group-specific)
  dpds2 ~ c(beta_pds_m, beta_pds_f)*pds1
  dpds3 ~ c(beta_pds_m, beta_pds_f)*pds2.5

  ddc2 ~ c(beta_dc_m, beta_dc_f)*dc1
  ddc3 ~ c(beta_dc_m, beta_dc_f)*dc2.5

  ### change-on-change (momentum)
  dpds3 ~ c(phi_pds_m, phi_pds_f)*dpds2
  ddc3  ~ c(phi_dc_m, phi_dc_f)*ddc2

  ### coupling effects
  ', if (delta) {
    'dpds2 ~ c(delta1_m, delta1_f)*dc1
     dpds3 ~ c(delta2_m, delta2_f)*dc2.5'
  } else '', '

  ', if (xi) {
    'ddc2 ~ c(xi1_m, xi1_f)*pds1
     ddc3 ~ c(xi2_m, xi2_f)*pds2.5'
  } else '', '

  ### latent change decomposition
  pds2 ~ 1*dpds2
  pds3 ~ 1*dpds3
  dc2  ~ 1*ddc2
  dc3  ~ 1*ddc3

  ### intercepts
  pds1 ~ 1
  dc1 ~ 1

  ### latent variances
  pds1 ~~ c(v_pds1_m, v_pds1_f)*pds1
  dc1  ~~ c(v_dc1_m, v_dc1_f)*dc1
  dpds2 ~~ c(v_dpds2_m, v_dpds2_f)*dpds2
  dpds3 ~~ c(v_dpds3_m, v_dpds3_f)*dpds3
  ddc2  ~~ c(v_ddc2_m, v_ddc2_f)*ddc2
  ddc3  ~~ c(v_ddc3_m, v_ddc3_f)*ddc3

  ### residual variances
  PDSS_fu1 ~~ PDSS_fu1
  PDSS_fu2 ~~ PDSS_fu2
  PDSS_fu4 ~~ PDSS_fu4
  disc_mean_fu1 ~~ disc_mean_fu1
  disc_mean_fu2 ~~ disc_mean_fu2
  disc_mean_fu4 ~~ disc_mean_fu4

  PDSS_fu1 ~~ disc_mean_fu1
  PDSS_fu2 ~~ disc_mean_fu2
  PDSS_fu4 ~~ disc_mean_fu4

  ### time-varying covariates
  dpds2 ~ age_fu1 + age_fu2
  dpds3 ~ age_fu2
  ddc2  ~ age_fu1 + age_fu2
  ddc3  ~ age_fu2

  ### time-invariant covariates
  #pds1 ~ site_id_l
  #dc1  ~ site_id_l
  pds1 ~ age_fu1
  dc1  ~ age_fu1

  ### changes made from MI
  pds1 ~~ dc1
  ')

  # fit the model
  fit <- tryCatch(
    lavaan::sem(
      model_code,
      data = data_wide,
      group = "sex",
      estimator = "MLR",
      missing = "fiml",
      fixed.x = FALSE
    ),
    error = function(e) e
  )

  model_list[[model_name]] <- fit
}

Happy to provide more information if needed!

Thanks in advance,

Clare

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have been struggling very long with a tiny detail in compRelSEM function (and previously in reliability/reliabilityL2 functions), which has big consequences on the easiness of analytical workflow. Therefore, I have a request for a brief but serious improvement.

If any CFA model is fitted, reverse-coded items are not any problem; they just have negative factor loadings (and "reversed" intercepts/thresholds, which does not impact reliability estimates).

However, when estimating reliability using compRelSEM, each item has a "weight" 1 (thus, there is a simple sum of factor loadings and residual variances in the equation). However, if reverse-coded items are present, this approach obviously lead to meaningless results.

My suggestion is adding a "key" parameter providing manual item weights (default value would be vector of repeated "1"), which could be +1 and -1, or even 0(!) or any other value if reliability of weigted item sum is desired. Then, each row in lambda matrix should be multiplied by this weights, i.e.
lambda <- lambda * keys
theta matrix should by multiplied by the keying cross-product, i.e.
theta <- theta* t(t(keys)) %*% t(keys)
and finaly the total score with obs.var = TRUE should be the weighted sum (I could forget something; not sure about Green-Yang ordinal correction).

This would be very helpful as recently, I have to fit a new model with reverse-coded items to obtain reliability.
This improvement could also serve for excluding variables from the reliability estimation, or weightening, if number of points per item differ (which is not a problem for estimating omega with continuous items, but is a serious problem in ordinal CFA now).

What do you think about that?

messages.subject: Question on Scalar Invariance Testing Accounting for Age Effects
messages.subject_clean: Question on Scalar Invariance Testing Accounting for Age Effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am using a longitudinal CFA to model a latent construct (small vessel disease - SVD) that is measured by 3 MRI indicators. My initial goal is to test the measurement invariance of that model over two time points (baseline and follow-up). Even though the configural and metric invariance models hold, the scalar invariance model is rejected. My suspicion is that this is due to factors other than SVD influencing the indicators over time. The first one that comes to mind is age (also, the age effect might be different for each indicator, and might also be different across the two time points).

In an attempt to account for that age effect, I incorporated a set of regressions in the model, where I basically regress each indicator on age. Then, the fit of the scalar invariance model improves significantly.

This, in my mind, is a similar approach of using residuals to partial out the age effect from each MRI indicator, but I also incorporate these regressions in the model so the overall fit can be tested.

I would really appreciate your input on whether this approach is correct or testing scalar invariance using this model is not valid for some reason.

Thank you in advance!

This is the parametrization I'm using (I'm including only the scalar invariance model for brevity):

model <-('
ind1_t1 ~ age.1
ind1_t2 ~ age.2
ind2_t1 ~ age.1
ind2_t2 ~ age.2
ind3_t1 ~ age.1
ind3_t2 ~ age.2

age.1 ~~ age.2

# Measurement model for svd in time 1
 svd_1 =~ 1*ind1_t1 + l2*ind2_t1 + l3*ind3_t1

# Measurement model for svd in time 2
 svd_2 =~ 1*ind1_t2 + l2*ind2_t2 + l3*ind3_t2

# Mean structure specification
ind1_t1 ~ i1*1
ind2_t1 ~ i2*1
ind3_t1 ~ i3*1
ind1_t2 ~ i1*1
ind2_t2 ~ i2*1
ind3_t2 ~ i3*1

# Residual covariances
ind1_t1  ~~  ind1_t2
ind2_t1  ~~  ind2_t2
ind3_t1  ~~  ind3_t2

# Latent variable means
svd_1 ~ 0*1
svd_2 ~ 1')

fit <- lavaan::sem(model, data = dat, estimator = "MLR")

Hello,

I am estimating the latent correlation between two measurement models on multiple imputed datasets: one with a two-factor model ("pos" and "neg") and another with only one factor. I am ultimately interested in the pos-swl and neg-swl factor correlations. As displayed below, I am using cfa.mi() to accomplish this:

sc.swl.1 <- '#specifying measurement model portion
pos  =~ NA*SCS_SF_q2 + SCS_SF_q5 + SCS_SF_q10  + SCS_SF_q3 + SCS_SF_q7
neg =~ NA*SCS_SF_q11 + SCS_SF_q4 + SCS_SF_q8 + SCS_SF_q1 + SCS_SF_q9
pos ~~ 1*pos
neg ~~ 1*neg

swl =~ NA*SWLS_q1 + SWLS_q2 + SWLS_q3 + SWLS_q4 + SWLS_q5
swl ~~ 1*swl

#specifying structural model portion
  pos ~~ swl
  neg ~~ swl'
sc.swl.1.out = sem.mi(sc.swl.1, data=imp2final, ordered=c("SCS_SF_q1", "SCS_SF_q2", "SCS_SF_q3", "SCS_SF_q4", "SCS_SF_q5", "SCS_SF_q7", "SCS_SF_q8", "SCS_SF_q9", "SCS_SF_q10", "SCS_SF_q11", "SWLS_q1", "SWLS_q2", "SWLS_q3", "SWLS_q4", "SWLS_q5"), estimator = "WLSMV", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)
summary(sc.swl.1.out, standardized = TRUE, rsquare=TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)

The output indicates it ran fine with no accompanying warnings:

> summary(sc.swl.1.out, standardized = TRUE, rsquare=TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)
lavaan.mi object fit to 20 imputed data sets using:
 - lavaan    (0.6-19)
 - lavaan.mi (0.1-0)
See class?lavaan.mi help page for available methods.

The model converged on 20 imputed data sets.
Standard errors were available for all imputations.

  Estimator                                       DWLS
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of model parameters                        88

  Number of observations                           170

But, when I consult my correlation residual and standardized residual matrices with lavResiduals.mi(), I get 22 warning messages saying this repeatedly:

There were 22 warnings (use warnings() to see them)
> warnings()
Warning messages:
1: lavaan->lav_model_vcov():
   The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov) does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue (= -2.644786e-18) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

I consulted vcov() but not sure if that is helping to diagnose the problem. I read on Stack Overflow (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/69911717/cfa-in-r-the-variance-covariance-matrix-of-the-estimated-parameters-vcov-does) that this might instead be a "warning about possible linear dependencies (redundancies) among some combination of model parameters." But that in lieu of no identification issues (which I don't think is the problem with my SEM), this might also reflect issues with my sample size and using DWLS.

I am wondering about the seeming disconnect between the okay output from lavaan.mi() with no indication of NPD and the nature of the warning messages popping up when lavResiduals.mi()is called. Want to make sure I'm not missing a major red flag with the model.

Thanks,
Bryan

If the model is not identified that is a problem, but diagnosing whether a model is identified in software is not always straightforward (or possible). The way to tell is to run the model with different starting values (be sure to set the same seed if using something like imputation) - if it converges to different values, the model is not identified and that's a problem. If it converges to the same results, you're probably OK.

But that is a pretty small sample for DWLS.

Hope that helps, at least a little,

Jeremy

messages.subject_clean: Pooled CFA for measurement invariance?
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

My ultimate goal is to compare SEMs for different groups by making a model for each group that looks something like this (the "structural equations" section is the most important part for the set-up, but I'm certainly open to feedback if my model construction has issues!):

model <- '

  # Define latent variables

  A =~ a1 + a2 + a3 + a4 + a5 + a6

  B =~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4

  #variances and covariances

  A ~~ A

  B ~~ B

  # Structural equations

  B ~ A

  MeasuredOutcomeVar ~ A + B

'

Before I run my SEM, I want to establish measurement invariance for my two latent variables, A and B, using the cfa() function. I am not sure if I should do this separately or together. I'm not including them here, but understand how to test for different levels of measurement invariance.

Together would look like this, whereas separate would be A alone and then B alone:

cfa_model <- '
  A =~ a1 + a2 + a3 + a4 + a5 + a6
  B =~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4

  # Correlations
  A ~~ B
'
cfa(cfa_model, data = data, meanstructure = TRUE)

I have heard this referred to as a pooled CFA. I am not sure if I've seen it done so much in a measurement invariance context. Ultimately I want to make sure that the terms of my SEMs (as well as the means of my latent variables) are comparable across groups.

Do you have any advice or further reading for me?
Thank you so much!

P.S.

A separate but related question: when if ever is pooled cfa appropriate for measurement invariance. We collected a lot of items informing a lot (~10) of latent variables as part of a study. Would it be appropriate to test for measurement invariance for them all at once? Or will this basically make it invalid and difficult to know which latent variables have invariance issues.

Also, what do you do when your latent variable is informed by three items and so you cannot get RMSEA, CFI, etc? The chi-squared seems overly sensitive due to our sample size. I could imagine pooling helping us with this issue, but I want to know if that's a valid choice and if not what to do instead to assess measurement invariance for this latent variable.

messages.subject_clean: Multiple imputation (mice) in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
I have a question regarding the alignment between model specification in lavaan for structural equation modelling (SEM) and the model specification used during multiple imputation with mice.
For my study, I’m using a longitudinal dataset to examine the relationship between variable X in childhood and outcome Y in adulthood, with a focus on the mediating role of M that was measured between X and Y. I plan to handle missing data using multiple imputation and conduct the SEM analysis using lavaan.mi.
One challenge I’m currently facing is how to correctly specify the imputation model. The literature seems somewhat unclear about whether it is appropriate to include outcome variables (like Y) when imputing missing values in variables measured earlier (such as X or M). Is it necessary to preserve the temporal order of variables in the imputation model like in the SEM model, or is it acceptable, and perhaps advisable, to include all available variables, regardless of measurement time, to improve the imputation?

Thank you very much in advance for your help.

Best wishes,
Ahmad

messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

1) "fitted(fit)$cov" will indeed give you the (cov)ariance matrix implied by the model.
2) Just use "cov(Data)" (from base R). "vcov" as in "lavInspect(fit, "vcov")" will give you a matrix that contains the (cov)ariance matrix of the estimated model parameters. This information could be useful for computing the SEs of certain parameters, for instance.

This link (https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/lavInspect.html) contains the answer to your questions and more. For instance, "lavInspect(fit, "cov.ov")" would give you the same as "fitted(fit)$cov".

3) The theta matrix contains the (cov)ariances of the residuals (measurement errors) for the observed variables. I may have misinterpreted your question, but if you want the difference between the observed (cov)ariance matrix and the model implied (cov)variance matrix, then "lavResiduals(fit)" should do it.

Check this link as well: https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/lavResiduals.html

Best,
Felipe.

On Thu, 24 Apr 2025 at 03:49, Michael Filsecker <filsec...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hey Felipe,
>
> that was awesome! I will check it out:) BTW, I wonder what are the reasons, I am not a statistician, that this re-scaling (N-1/N) seems to be SO important?? and the other similar questions why seems to be a big deal if you divided by N-1 versus N??
>

I think it's debated. Some SEM programs do it, and some do not.

> My last question I can not understand clearly, why a just identified model has a perfect fit? I just do not get the link between the two :(
>

There isn't a link between the two. They are the same thing.

In a SEM you are testing whether you can reproduce the sample covariance matrix (and means, but we'll ignore that).

Think of a super simple SEM, with two variables: y1 and y2. They have variance  = 1 and covariance = 0.3

My model, in Lavaan, is:

y1 ~~ y2

I've put one covariance into the model, and I've asked the model to estimate one covariance - that of y1 and y2. The model is saturated; it has 0 degrees of freedom and will have perfect fit (chi-square = 0), because it will exactly reproduce the data. It might be an interesting finding, but it is not an interesting structural equation model.

You can think of lots of statistical methods: t-test, anova, regression, ancova, manova, logistic regression, etc as structural equation models. They are all saturated and have perfect fit - so we don't worry about what it is (although sometimes we think about the log likelihood and calculate things like AIC). In those models we are only interested in the parameter estimates (and their CIs, etc), in SEMs we are interested in fit and parameters.

I hope that helps, a little.

Jeremy

P.S. I wrote a paper once about the equivalence of SEMs and other techniques - calculating power in SEMs is easier than calculating power in (say) MANOVA, so we can take advantage of the fact that  the models are the same: https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2288-3-27.

On 4/24/25 12:49, Michael Filsecker wrote:
> reasons, I am not a statistician, that this re-scaling (N-1/N) seems to
> be SO important?? and the other similar questions why seems to be a big
> deal if you divided by N-1 versus N??

In the early days of SEM, when SEM was just covariance structure
analysis, they were using maximum likelihood estimation based on the
Wishart distribution of the sample covariance matrix ('S'). In this
setting, theory dictates you need to use N-1.

But the Wishart distribution only applies when data is complete. If you
have missing data, we need to switch to the normal distribution. But the
normal theory dictates we should use N (instead of N-1).

Software (like lavaan and Mplus) that use the normal distribution for
the missing values case, also use the normal distribution (per default)
for the complete case. That just seems more consistent. Hence, lavaan
(and Mplus) insist on using 'N' whenever maximum likelihood is used.
This includes the computation of the sample covariance matrix.

(BTW, if your data is complete, you can use the likelihood = "Wishart"
option to switch to the Wishart setting, if you prefer this)

Yves.

--

Department of Data Analysis, Ghent University

>
> In the early days of SEM, when SEM was just covariance structure
> analysis, they were using maximum likelihood estimation based on the
> Wishart distribution of the sample covariance matrix ('S'). In this
> setting, theory dictates you need to use N-1.
>
> But the Wishart distribution only applies when data is complete. If you
> have missing data, we need to switch to the normal distribution. But the
> normal theory dictates we should use N (instead of N-1).
>
> Software (like lavaan and Mplus) that use the normal distribution for
> the missing values case, also use the normal distribution (per default)
> for the complete case. That just seems more consistent. Hence, lavaan
> (and Mplus) insist on using 'N' whenever maximum likelihood is used.
> This includes the computation of the sample covariance matrix.
>
> (BTW, if your data is complete, you can use the likelihood = "Wishart"

Dear all,
I’m new to mediation analysis with imputed datasets, and I have a question concerning pooling estimates and obtaining confidence intervals (CIs) for indirect effects using semTools::monteCarloCI.

Initially, I tried to estimate the indirect effect CI using bootstrapping with sem.mi:
med_bootresd <- sem.mi(model=hypo1_imp, data = impList_Comp,
                           ordered = c("Dru_Adh","cdvl_su"),
                           se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = 5000, estimator = "DWLS",
                           verbose = TRUE)
This produced the following error:
Error in lavaan.mi::lavaan.mi(model = hypo1_imp, data = impList_Comp, : Bootstraping unavailable (and not recommended) in combination with multiple imputations. For robust confidence intervals of indirect effects, see the ?semTools::monteCarloCI help page. To bootstrap within each imputation, users can pass a custom function to the FUN= argument (see ?lavaanList) to save bootstrap distributions in the @funList slot, then manually combine afterward.

Based on the error, I would like to use monteCarloCI instead of manual bootstrapping.
My question is: if I should use MonteCarloCI, do I need to include the number of replications as with bootstrapping, because the help page doesn’t explicitly mention the nRep argument?
Example:
FITimp <- sem.mi(hypo1_imp, data = impList_Comp,
                        ordered = c("Dru_Adh","cdvl_su"),
                        estimator = "DWLS")
mc_results <- monteCarloCI(FITimp, nRep = 5000, seed = 12345).

Thank you!

Sandra

Hi Sandra,

Yes, nRep controls the number of replications to draw from the distributions of each parameter to form confidence intervals for a new parameter. Recommendations for replication a Monte Carlo CI are usually much higher than what's used in bootstrapping. The default in monteCarloCI is 20,000 replications but if you want more precision doing more replications doesn't hurt anything.

Here's a tutorial a couple of colleagues and I wrote about testing indirect effects with missing data that provides some background on these methods. The examples use mediation models with observed variables but everything also applies to latent variables.

Alex

messages.subject: Re: model with formative and reflexive indicators
messages.subject_clean: model with formative and reflexive indicators
messages.body_plain:
I don't know of any SEM software that can fit that model - it is not identified (without a lot of constraints).

If you think about this in path tracing terms, the effect from:

x1 to y3 = x1 -> y1 * y1 -> y3
x2 to y3 = x2 -> y1 * y1 -> y3
x3 to y3 = x3 -> y1 * y1 -> y3

The path from y1 -> y3 is not doing anything here - it's just a multiplier - it could double in value, and the formative effects from x1:x3 to y1 would halve, and the model would be identical.

To identify the model, first, remove the latent variables y1 and y2, and regression y3 directly on x1:x6.

It's still problematic - y4 only has one indicator. That has no error variance, and you need to constrain its loading to 1. But that means that it is equivalent to it being an indicator of y3. y4 isn't doing anything (except making your model more complex).

Jeremy

With p indicators for a factor, you replace the p residual variances with p - 1 additional variables, so that the p observed variables are represented by p new variables, making the p new variables composites. The github version of lavaan (0.6-20) has improved support for
composites. The goal is to allow for a seamless integration of both
latent variables and composites in the same model.

Try this toy example (after you have installed the github version):

library(lavaan)

# generate some data
pop.model <- '
   eta1 <~ 1*x11 + 0.4*x12 + 0.6*x13
   eta2 =~ 1*x21 + 0.8*x22 + 0.9*x23
   eta3 <~ 1*x31 + 0.2*x32 + 0.5*x33 + 0.3*x34
   eta4 =~ 1*x41 + 0.7*x42 + 0.8*x43

   # indicators composites
   x11 ~~ 6*x11
   x12 ~~ 5*x12
   x13 ~~ 2*x13

   x31 ~~ 7*x31
   x32 ~~ 3*x32
   x33 ~~ 2*x33
   x34 ~~ 5*x34

   x11 ~~ 2*x12 + 1.2*x13
   x12 ~~ 1.5*x13

   x31 ~~ 0.9*x32
   x31 ~~ 0.5*x33
   x31 ~~ 1.2*x34
   x32 ~~ 0.7*x33
   x32 ~~ 1.8*x34
   x33 ~~ 0.5*x34

   # indicators latent variables
   x21 ~~ 0.5*x21
   x22 ~~ 0.5*x22
   x23 ~~ 0.5*x23

   x41 ~~ 0.5*x41
   x42 ~~ 0.5*x42
   x43 ~~ 0.5*x43

   # latent variances
   eta2 ~~ 1*eta2
   eta4 ~~ 1*eta4

   # structural part
   eta3 ~ 0.5*eta1 + 0.6*eta2
   eta4 ~ 0.1*eta1 + 0.3*eta3 + 0.2*eta2

   eta1 ~~ 0.1*eta2
'
Data <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 200L, empirical = TRUE)

# fit a model with both latent variables and composites
model <- '
  eta1 <~ x11 + x12 + x13
  eta2 =~ x21 + x22 + x23
  eta3 <~ x31 + x32 + x33 + x34
  eta4 =~ x41 + x42 + x43

  # structural part
  eta3 ~ eta1 + eta2
  eta4 ~ eta1 + eta2 + eta3
'

fit <- sem(model, data = Data, verbose = TRUE,
            optim.gradient = "numerical")
summary(fit)

Note the use of optim.gradient = "numerical" when calling the sem()
function! That is because I have not derived the analytic gradient yet
for this setting.

A paper about the underlying methodology is under preparation.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
(Start with a bit of history).

When Lisrel was first written, computers were slow and memory was expensive.  So keeping the size of your matrices small was a good idea - it helped with memory and sped things up. When I factor analyzed the first data I collected for my PhD, I used to go for lunch, come back and hope it was finished. Now I blink and it has finished. No no there's no need to have 8 matrices, we can have fewer, large matrices. Our lives will be easier, but the computer's life will be harder (but computers are fast and cheap, and they are inaminate objects so we don't care).

(History over).

The vectors of endogenous and exogenous concepts (eta and ksi) are the latent variable variances (or unique variances), so that's one matrix, not two.  The structural coefficients (beta ) are the regressions among the latents,

Correlations among the latents (Gamma and Psi) are the correlations among the latents.

The observed endogenous (y) and exogenous (x) indicators are not just the indicators. The loadings (lambda-x and lambda-y) are just the loadings.

The variances and covariances of the endogenous variables (theta-epsilon and theta-delta) are the variances and covariances of the measured variables.

This sometimes led to all sorts of complications - if you wanted to correlate an exogenous latent variable with an endogenous latent variable, or regress an exogenous latent variable on another latent variable, you had to completley restructure your model (because that shifted xs to ys, and all sorts of downstream effects).  If you wanted a formative model, you couldn't regress a latent on a measured variable (there's no matrix for that) so you had to have each measured variable have it's own latent variable, with loading of 1 and no error variance.

You can (almost) think of the lavaan model as being a y-only model. The matrices are:

Loadings (lambda y)
Errors of measured variables (theta-epsilon)
Correlations of latent variables (psi)
Regressions of latent variables (gamma).

You still can't fit formative measures (where an arrow points from a measured variable to a latent variable) into this framework without creating extra latent variables that you don't really want though. If you do this, you'll have some big, sparse matrices to multiply. But you 're not doing it, so that's OK.

Jeremy

If you Google that error message you'll find it comes up a lot, in a lot of different sorts of package (Google found about 40 pages that mentioned it, and 5 of them mention Lavaan). I don't think it's a lavaan problem (although it's possible that code could be added to check for it), it's an error that's thrown by the matrix() function in base R.

One great thing about R being open source is that anyone can propose a fix (to matrix, or Lavaan) to fix it. A less great thing about R being open source is that it is no one's job to do that.

Another great thing about R is that you can build upon other people's packages to create your own - you don't need to start from scratch. A less great thing is that you are relying on those packages handling errors nicely.

(This used to happen in Mplus and Mx [it might still, I haven't used them in a long time], sometimes you get a nice error message from Mplus, sometimes you get something completely incomprehensible from a Fortran routine. At least with R you can dig into the code and work out what the problem might be - if you spend long enough.

Can you post all of your code so that we can reproduce the error?

Thanks,

Jeremy
